rust.note: Both programs have a quiet main entry and print one line. Grail uses a builtin function call; Rust println! is a formatting macro. Grail uses checked call-scoped borrowing so owners remain usable after println.

Grail distinguishes immutable declarations (base := 40), mutable declarations (mut answer = base), and assignment (=). Rust uses let and let mut. Both require explicit mutable permission for reassignment.

Both infer the literal bindings' types from later use: full becomes u8 at the call, and sum takes i32 from its first sized update. Grail treats an immutable literal binding like the literal itself at each use (with a range check there); a mutable one gets the type of its first sized use anywhere in the function, recompiling the function if that use comes after code was already generated. Rust infers one type per binding from all uses.

Both are checked: overflow and division by zero stop the program (these Rust comparisons build with overflow-checks=on and panic=abort; Rust release builds wrap by default). Grail's explicit wrapping_add/wrapping_sub correspond to Rust's wrapping_* methods. bool is its own type in both languages.

Both use if/else for branching. Rust can return the value of an if expression; Grail uses explicit returns here. Both require a `bool` condition and both produce `bool` from a comparison, so an integer is refused where a condition is expected.
Grail for i in n iterates from zero up to n, excluding n; Rust spells that range 0..n. Both support while, break and continue, and require an explicit mutable binding for updates.

Both loops move each owned element out of the vector, so the vector is consumed and each iteration owns the string it reads; borrowing the second vector with `&kept` leaves it usable afterwards, including its length. Grail writes `string[]` where Rust writes `Vec<String>`.

examples.diagnostic: a condition must be a bool

rust.note: Both languages require a `bool` condition: an integer is not a truth value in either, and the fix is `if level != 0`. Grail's comparisons produce `bool`, and `bool` and integers do not mix in arithmetic or comparison, so there is no quiet integer-to-condition path.
Both support native recursion. Rust can return a trailing expression; Grail uses return for non-unit results and allows implicit unit returns. This example makes no performance claim.

Both initialize an owned byte buffer with a literal, then borrow it readonly; neither needs a mutable binding here. Grail bytes is specialized, while Rust uses Vec<u8>. Growth would require mut / let mut respectively.
Both lengths count UTF-8 bytes. Grail string literals here are owned strings; Rust string literals are borrowed static str values, so this comparison explicitly constructs a String.

Both ranges are half-open and bounds-checked. Rust slices are borrowed pointer/length values. A view of a runtime value is a descriptor the runtime allocates and releases; only a literal's view is built at compile time, so do not infer zero-allocation views from this syntax.
Both transfer owned buffers by move and clean up the callee-owned value. Grail’s affine ownership is not presented as something Rust lacks.
Both reject using an owner after a move. Repair either version by using the new owner, borrowing, or explicitly cloning/copying data.
Both can end a borrow at last use. Rust calls this non-lexical lifetimes; this is a shared capability, not a Grail-only feature.
Both reject vector growth while a reader is still live. Reallocation would invalidate that reader.

borrow(...) of a temporary works like Rust's &temporary: the value is kept alive until the end of the enclosing block, so start can be used after its statement. The borrow checker still rejects returning it or keeping it past that block.

Rust spells this slice reborrow &*writer; Grail spells its byte-view reborrow &writer. Both suspend conflicting exclusive access until the readonly child’s last use. The example writes with write(view, i, b); Grail also accepts view[i] = b, like Rust.
Grail exchange and load make storage operations explicit. Rust uses a standard-library replace function and dereference syntax; both return the old value without losing its ownership.

Both return their only input view. Grail elides the lifetime on both sides: every elided input gets a fresh lifetime, and a sole input lifetime flows to an elided output. Rust could elide it too; it is written explicitly here to show the relationship. Rust shared references are Copy; Grail view handles passed by value are affine and may require explicit derivation.
Both reject returning a view into a local owner, even though the signature declares an input lifetime. A lifetime annotation cannot keep that allocation alive.

Both support partial moves and drop the remaining owned fields. Both use field punning: Message { body, label } names each field once. Rust’s String construction makes the owned-text comparison explicit.
Grail .pop() aborts on an empty vector. Rust Vec::pop returns Option, letting ordinary code handle emptiness instead of unwrapping it. Both protect element references from reallocation.

Both match tagged variants and move owned payloads into an arm. Rust qualifies variant patterns; Grail uses unqualified names in a consuming match. bool is its own type in both languages and the same `if flag` picks the variant in each.

Rust uses Result; Grail uses a structural u8[] |? string result. A member value is returned directly, ? propagates a failure member to a matching failure alternative, and member patterns name the payload (data: u8[]). Grail ! aborts on failure; Rust unwrap panics and this verifier uses panic=abort.
Matching through borrow(slot) binds payloads as references. As in Rust, the borrow ends at the payload's last use, so the arm may then assign slot. Using n after the assignment is rejected.

Grail uses the named Holder record and T? optional syntax; Rust uses Pair and Option. Both infer the generic arguments from the fields. A payload-free None needs context or an explicit type argument; Grail writes None. Both support the partial move here.
Grail writes identity<u64>; Rust uses a turbofish, identity::<u64>. Both infer the buffer instantiation and specialize generic code.
Both reject this unconstrained generic body even when called with a copyable integer. Rust can opt into T: Copy or Clone bounds; Grail does not yet offer that trait mechanism.

Both must preserve the lifetime of the newly stored borrow. Rust elides the slot lifetime here. Grail’s current weak-update checker may retain old guards longer, and rejects some opaque external writes that Rust can express.

Both call arithmetic::twice from a separate source file shown below. Grail dependencies declare their module and are passed explicitly to the compiler. Rust mod arithmetic associates arithmetic.rs through its module/file rules; neither helper is a standalone program.

Both require exactly one user argument, exit with status 2 otherwise, and count its raw Unix bytes rather than Unicode characters. Grail passes the one argument to main as a read-only byte view, spelled &[u8]; Rust reads args_os and uses the Unix OsStrExt byte view. This is a Linux/Unix comparison, not a portable Windows argv claim.

Both perform fail-fast byte-oriented file I/O: read note.txt, write copy.txt and print the contents plus byte length. Grail read_file aborts on error and asserts a zero write status. Rust uses expect on io::Result and the verifier selects panic=abort; it is not demonstrating recoverable ? propagation here.

Both run /bin/true without a shell and print its normal exit status. Grail consumes an owned vector of byte arguments; Rust uses Command. Launch failures differ: Grail encodes an error in its numeric result, while Rust returns io::Result. This example tests normal completion on Linux/Unix.

Both refuse a path outside their root and a write without write permission, and print the same three results. Grail's Authority is a value that carries the grant, so a read-only authority refuses the write in the language; Rust's std has no capability type, so this program writes through a read-only file handle and the operating system refuses it. Neither program can reach ../outside.txt.

Both deterministically destroy owners on normal exits, including continue and early return. Rust supports custom Drop; Grail uses generated default cleanup. The flag is a `bool` in both languages, so each program drops the same values on the same path. No relative allocation/performance claim follows from this example.
Both reject mutating an owned buffer through an immutable binding. Grail uses := for immutable declarations and mut for mutable ones; Rust uses let and let mut.

Both examples use checked arithmetic in the verification profile. Grail has right-associative ** and **=; Rust uses checked_pow for the same intent. Explicit wrapping_pow requests modular arithmetic in both. Grail also offers --overflow=wrap for user code; runtime and bounds guards stay checked. ^ is XOR in both.

Both run four tasks on OS threads and join them before continuing. Rust uses scoped closures and a MutexGuard; Grail uses parallel_map context values and scopes mutex access to a callback. Grail closures capture by value, so shared state is passed explicitly.

`parallel_for_chunks(&mut data[0: 10], 3, f)` splits an exclusive slice into disjoint exclusive chunks: size = ceil(n/chunks), so ten elements over three chunks is 4, 4 and 2, and each job writes the caller's own elements. Rust has no pool in `std`, so the twin is `chunks_mut(4)` - the same arithmetic split - with one scoped thread per chunk; `thread::scope` joins them before the vector is read, exactly as the Grail call joins its jobs. Neither program copies an element, and the second pass shows the same shape at `chunks_mut(5)` through `pool::chunks_mut`.

`parallel_spawn(f)` returns a `Job<R>` and `parallel_join(job)` takes the owned result; `std::thread::spawn` and `JoinHandle::join` are the same two steps in Rust, and a handle is move-only and owned by the thread that waits on it in both. The handle may outlive the statement that started the work, and a result belongs to its own handle, so joining two live jobs in the reverse of their start order prints the same numbers in both languages. Grail refuses a callback that captured a borrow for the same reason Rust's `'static` bound does: the handle records the result type, not the closure's lifetimes.

Both check overflow by default and require explicit conversions between widths. Grail infers an unsuffixed literal from the other operand; Rust infers it from the declared type. wrapping_u8(300) and 300u16 as u8 both keep the low eight bits.

Grail closures behave like Rust move closures: captures are copied or moved into the closure and read in its body. Grail writes the closure type Fn(u64) -> u64 directly; Rust uses impl Fn or generics. Closures that capture a reference or view, and closures that write a capture (`FnMut`), are both supported; a struct or enum that merely holds a borrow is still not capturable.

A Grail closure that writes a captured value is FnMut: the binding that holds it is declared mut, and calling it borrows the closure exclusively, so two calls cannot overlap. Rust infers FnMut from the body the same way; Grail spells the type FnMut(u64) -> u64 where a parameter needs to name it.

Rust names the protocol as a trait with an associated Item type; Grail has no traits, so `for` looks for an inherent `next(self: &mut Self) -> T?` structurally. `for p in &mut it` lends the iterator in both, and the borrowing iterator keeps its vector borrowed in both.

rust.note: Rust's adapters are trait methods chained with dots and monomorphised per closure; Grail's are functions over a closure-backed Iter<T>, so a chain reads inside-out and each step is an indirect call. Both are lazy: take(3) stops the 900-item range after three items.

Grail writes the receiver as an ordinary first parameter (self: &mut Counter) where Rust uses &mut self; both borrow the receiver automatically at the call site, and both can reuse a field name in a struct literal.

rust.note: A Grail show method plays the role of Rust's Display implementation. Grail's 'G' is a byte (71), matching Rust's b'G'; Grail also has a `char`: `'G'` is a byte literal and `'ï'` would be a character.

Both print the shortest decimal that reads back to the same double. Grail requires explicit conversions in both directions (f64(n), i64(x)); i64(x) truncates like Rust's as, but stops the program for NaN or out-of-range values instead of saturating.

char is a Unicode scalar value and chars() decodes UTF-8 like Rust. An ASCII literal such as 'g' is still a byte value (Rust's b'g') unless a char context like initial: char adopts it; 'ï' is always a char. f32 arithmetic rounds every result to binary32 and prints the shortest digits that read back as the same f32.

Grail's [K: V] map supports literals and required-key indexing: map[key] aborts when the key is missing, map[key] = value upserts, and map[key] += value updates an existing key. get, get_mut and entry are the optional forms; entry is an optional Entry view (shared key, mutable value) and never inserts, so moving a non-copyable value out uses remove. Rust's HashMap uses the same indexing form and returns Option from get. Grail sorts through the imported order::Ord interface; Rust passes a comparison closure to sort_by.

rust.note: Grail iterates a map by position: `for key, value in &m` holds one shared borrow of the map for the loop, so the body can read every pair but cannot grow the map. `&mut m` yields the same shared key with an exclusive value, so values update in place while the keys stay readable. Rust's iter and iter_mut draw the same line, but std's HashMap has no order: Grail keeps insertion order, so this comparison uses a BTreeMap with keys inserted in sorted order.

rust.note: Both sorts are stable. Rust's comparator returns an Ordering; Grail's returns whether the first element comes first, the same convention as C++'s std::stable_sort. Grail string literals are owned text, so no .to_string() is needed.

The same C file, the same two shapes. Rust's `#[repr(C)]` states the layout, `*const AppInfo` in a field is Grail's `CPtr` field (and borrow checking is Rust's own: `p_app: &app` keeps the reference alive for the call), and `&mut filled` is the `struct app_info *` `book_fill` writes. `AppInfo { api_version: 0, flags: 0 }` is the value Grail's `mut filled: AppInfo;` ends up with: the callee wrote `api_version`, and `flags` is the zero the storage started as.

examples.diagnostic: cannot assign to `app` while a C pointer to it is live in `info`

rust.note: Both reject replacing the record while a create-info still points at it. Rust needs a lifetime on the struct to say so (a raw `*const AppInfo` has none, which is why ash's `InstanceCreateInfo<'a>` carries one); Grail's `CPtr` field holds the borrow `cptr(&app)` took, so the plain record type is enough.

A record of `handle` fields is the array C writes: `c_alloc_buffers(&mut buffers)` is the `struct command_buffers *`, and the same record goes back to C as a parameter without a copy. Rust has no handle type, so the twin stores words and spells the same rule with `MaybeUninit`: the storage exists for C to write, and `assume_init` is the point where the bytes become a value. Both programs print the same four numbers, including the identity check between the handle Grail read out of the array and the one C handed back.

examples.diagnostic: use of moved, borrowed or partially initialized value

rust.note: Both languages refuse to read a field of a binding that nothing has written, for the same reason: the value does not exist yet. Grail's storage is `sizeof(struct)` zeroed bytes, so `&mut caps` is a valid pointer for C to fill and a field C leaves alone reads 0 - but reading a field before a foreign call or an assignment wrote one is a partially initialized value. Rust's uninitialised binding is the same error under another name (E0381), and `MaybeUninit` is Rust's spelling of the zeroed-but-unwritten state Grail gives an `extern "C"` record by default.

examples.diagnostic: byval must name an extern "C" record

rust.note: Rust passes a `#[repr(C)]` struct by value and derives the C classification from the layout. Grail keeps a bare record parameter meaning the C `R *`, so passing a whole record is written `v: byval Vec2`, and the record must be declared `extern "C"`; asking for `byval` on an ordinary record is the rejection above. With both spellings satisfied the call compiles and executes on x86-64, AArch64 and RISC-V 64; Windows x86-64 and ARM64 refuse `byval` rather than guess MSVC's struct rules.
